sip.plain_english: A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) lets you invest a fixed small amount in a mutual fund every month instead of one big lump sum. Over time, you buy more units when the market is low and fewer when it's high — this averages out your cost.
sip.why_it_matters: SIPs are the easiest way for beginners to start investing because they remove the stress of timing the market. They also build the habit of regular saving.

affecting_entities.name: Net Asset Value (NAV)
affecting_entities.description: The per-unit price of the mutual fund. Each SIP installment buys units at the current NAV.

affecting_entities.name: Expense Ratio
affecting_entities.description: Annual fee charged by the fund house, expressed as a percentage of your investment. Higher expense ratio reduces your final returns.

affecting_entities.name: Fund Manager
affecting_entities.description: The person making investment decisions for the fund. A manager change can shift the fund's strategy and performance.

affecting_entities.name: Repo Rate (RBI Policy Rate)
affecting_entities.description: When RBI raises rates, debt funds usually lose value short-term but offer higher yields later; equity funds may slow down because borrowing is costlier.

affecting_entities.name: Inflation (CPI)
affecting_entities.description: If inflation is higher than your fund's return, your money loses real purchasing power.

affecting_entities.name: Market Volatility (NIFTY/SENSEX swings)
affecting_entities.description: Short-term swings affect NAV but SIPs naturally average them out over time. Beginners should focus on 3+ year horizons.

affecting_entities.name: Exit Load
affecting_entities.description: A small fee charged if you withdraw within a specified period (often 1 year). Reduces your effective returns if you exit early.

mutual_fund.plain_english: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and a professional manager invests it in stocks, bonds, or both. You own units of the fund instead of individual stocks.
mutual_fund.why_it_matters: Mutual funds give you instant diversification and professional management even with small amounts — you can't easily buy 50 stocks with ₹500 but a fund can.

affecting_entities.name: Net Asset Value (NAV)
affecting_entities.description: Daily price per unit. Calculated from the underlying holdings' market value minus expenses.

affecting_entities.name: Expense Ratio
affecting_entities.description: Annual cost. A 2% expense ratio means ₹2 of every ₹100 invested goes to fund costs each year.

affecting_entities.name: Assets Under Management (AUM)
affecting_entities.description: Total money managed by the fund. Very small AUM means the fund might shut; very large AUM in small-cap funds can hurt performance.

affecting_entities.name: Underlying Market Performance
affecting_entities.description: Equity funds track NIFTY/SENSEX broadly; debt funds track bond yields. Their performance moves together.

stock.plain_english: A stock is a small piece of ownership in a company. If the company does well, the stock value goes up; if it does poorly, it goes down.
stock.why_it_matters: Stocks can give higher returns than fixed deposits or mutual funds, but they're also riskier. Individual stocks can lose 50%+ value while a diversified fund rarely does.

affecting_entities.name: Company Earnings
affecting_entities.description: Quarterly profit/loss reports. Better-than-expected earnings usually push the price up.

affecting_entities.name: Sector Performance
affecting_entities.description: All companies in the same sector (e.g., IT, banking) tend to move together when industry conditions change.

affecting_entities.name: Interest Rates
affecting_entities.description: Higher rates make borrowing costly for companies and make bonds more attractive than stocks, pulling stock prices down.

affecting_entities.name: Currency Exchange Rate
affecting_entities.description: Export-heavy companies (IT, pharma in India) benefit from a weaker rupee; import-heavy ones suffer.

affecting_entities.name: Global Market Sentiment
affecting_entities.description: Indian stocks often follow US market direction with a one-day lag — especially large-caps.

affecting_entities.name: Promoter Holdings
affecting_entities.description: If founders/promoters reduce their stake significantly, it can signal lack of confidence.

etf.plain_english: An ETF (Exchange Traded Fund) is like a mutual fund but trades on the stock exchange like a stock. It usually tracks an index (NIFTY 50, S&P 500) so you get diversification cheaply.
etf.why_it_matters: ETFs have much lower expense ratios than mutual funds (often 0.05% vs 1-2%) — that difference compounds massively over 10+ years. Best 'set and forget' option for beginners.

affecting_entities.name: Underlying Index Performance
affecting_entities.description: If you buy a NIFTY 50 ETF, your returns match NIFTY 50 minus a tiny fee.

affecting_entities.name: Tracking Error
affecting_entities.description: How closely the ETF follows its index. Lower is better — under 0.5% is good.

affecting_entities.name: Liquidity / Trading Volume
affecting_entities.description: Low-volume ETFs have wider bid-ask spreads, meaning you pay more to buy and get less to sell.

affecting_entities.name: Expense Ratio
affecting_entities.description: Annual fee. ETF expense ratios are usually 5-10x lower than mutual funds.

bond.plain_english: A bond is a loan you give to a government or company. They pay you fixed interest periodically and return your principal at maturity.
bond.why_it_matters: Bonds are predictable and safer than stocks. Good for the 'stable' portion of your portfolio, especially as you near goals like buying a house or retirement.

affecting_entities.name: Interest Rates (Repo / Fed Funds)
affecting_entities.description: When central banks raise rates, existing bond prices fall (new bonds offer better rates). When rates drop, bond prices rise.

affecting_entities.name: Credit Rating
affecting_entities.description: AAA bonds are safest; lower ratings (BBB and below) offer higher returns but higher default risk.

affecting_entities.name: Inflation
affecting_entities.description: High inflation erodes the real value of bond payments because they're typically fixed.

affecting_entities.name: Time to Maturity
affecting_entities.description: Longer-maturity bonds are more sensitive to rate changes. 10-year bonds swing more than 1-year bonds.

ncd.plain_english: A Non-Convertible Debenture (NCD) is a corporate bond — a loan you give to a company at a fixed interest rate for a fixed period. Issued by companies like HDFC, Muthoot, Shriram.
ncd.why_it_matters: NCDs often pay 1-3% higher interest than bank FDs because they're slightly riskier — you depend on the company staying solvent.

affecting_entities.name: Company Financial Health
affecting_entities.description: If the issuing company goes bankrupt, you may lose part or all of your principal.

affecting_entities.name: Credit Rating (CRISIL/ICRA)
affecting_entities.description: AAA-rated NCDs are very safe; AA and below get progressively riskier.

affecting_entities.name: Repo Rate
affecting_entities.description: If RBI hikes rates after you buy, your fixed-rate NCD becomes relatively less attractive.

affecting_entities.name: Liquidity in Secondary Market
affecting_entities.description: If you need to sell before maturity, NCDs can be hard to sell at a fair price.

fd.plain_english: A Fixed Deposit (FD) is money you lock in with a bank for a fixed period (e.g., 1 year) at a guaranteed interest rate. Withdraw early and you pay a small penalty.
fd.why_it_matters: FDs are the safest investment most beginners know — your principal is guaranteed (insured up to ₹5 lakh in India under DICGC). The tradeoff is low returns.

affecting_entities.name: Bank's Interest Rate
affecting_entities.description: Set by each bank, partly driven by RBI's repo rate. Compare across banks — small finance banks usually pay more.

affecting_entities.name: Inflation
affecting_entities.description: If your FD pays 7% and inflation is 6%, your real return is only 1%.

affecting_entities.name: Tax Bracket
affecting_entities.description: FD interest is fully taxable as income. A 30% tax bracket investor's 7% FD effectively becomes 4.9%.

affecting_entities.name: Bank Health
affecting_entities.description: Principal is insured only up to ₹5 lakh per bank per depositor. Spread large amounts across banks.
